title: A Highly Important Italian Violin, by Antonio Stradivari, Cremona, 1707
description: Labelled Antonius Stradiuarius Cremonensis Faciebat 1707, the handsome one-piece back of medium curl ascending slightly from left to right with original wings in the lower bouts, the ribs and head of broad curl, the table of narrow grain in the centre opening out to medium grain on the flanks of the treble side and broader grain on the flanks of the bass side, the varnish of a rich orange-red colour on a golden ground, length of back 35.6cm; 14in. Certificates: Hamma & Co., Stuttgart, dated 24th October 1949. W. E. Hill & Sons, London, dated 5th July 1955. Provenance: The violin is reputed to have at one time belonged to an officer in the army of Napoleon I from whom it was purchased by the first confirmed owner. This was the French Violinist Jean Baptiste Cartier (b. Avignon, 1765; d. Paris, 1841). Cartier was a pupil of Giovanni Battista Viotti, on whose recommendation he had formerly attained the post of Accompanist to Queen Marie-Antoinette. Between the years 1791 and 1821 he was assistant leader of the Paris Opéra orchestra and between 1804 and 1830 a member of the Court Orchestra thus he served under both the Napoleonic and Bourbon régimes. It was Cartier who named the violin ‘La Cathédrale’. In 1831 he sold the instrument to a Monsieur Pierre David, who in turn sold it in 1872 to Monsieur Lemoine, a businessman living in Paris. It passed into the family of the present owners in 1955.

title: A Rare and Interesting Viola, by Ernst Busch, Nuremberg 1641
description: Labelled Ernst Busch in Nürnberg A. 1641, the body of festoon outline, the two-piece back of wood cut on the slab of very faint medium curl with purfled decoration in the centre and below the button, the ribs of small-knotted bird’s eye maple, the table of fine grain in the centre opening out towards the flanks and pierced by modified flame sound holes and formerly by a rose beneath the fingerboard (now filled), double purfled and with marquetry flowers inlaid at the points of the festooning and around the rose, the pegbox of pearwood inlaid with boxwood stringing, with floral carving around the scroll and faced with a grotesque mask, the varnish of a red-brown colour, length of back 43.2cm; 17in, in baize bag (2). The work of Ernst Busch is represented in several European Collections but the most strikingly similar instrument to this viola is a division viol in the Musikinstrumenten-Museum der Karl-Marks-Universität Leipzig on which the same decorative techniques are employed. Because most surviving instruments by Busch are of the viol family, one might query whether this viola is in fact cut down from a small viol. There is however nothing about the instrument to indicate that this is what has happened. It is possible that the upper drops of the sound holes have been added although sound hole of the same design as the present ones are known on instruments by contemporary makers. For comparable instruments see Anthony Baines European and American Musical Instruments, pp. 18, 20 and pl. 106 and Carl Claudius Samling af Gamle Musikinstrumenter, Copenhagen, pp. 224 & 225.
